MR. CHAIRMAN: Q. No. 101.  Shri Manohar Joshi. ...(Interruptions)... 
Committee on private universities 
*101. SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of private universities established under various State legislations 
and whether they have acquired the status of research universities; 
(b) whether Government have received any suggestion from the University Grants 
Commission for constituting a high level committee to look into the fee and course 
structure of private universities; and 
(c) whether Government intend to set up some new Central universities, including 
some world class campuses, and if so, the number of such universities? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) According to available information, 12 private universities have been established 
by State Legislations, of which the University Grants Commission (UGC) has so far 
included 11 universities under Section 2(f) of the UGC Act, 1956 . The UGC does not 
confer status of Research Universities. Research in each university is governed by the 
concerned State legislation. 
(b) No Sir, the University Grants Commission (UGC) itself is empowered under the 
UGC Act, 1956 to make regulations, with the prior approval of the Central Government, 
for Admissions and Fee Structure in Universities and Colleges. In respect of Private 
Universities, the UGC (Establishment of and Maintenance of Standards in Private 
Universities) Regulations, 2003 have also been notified. 
(c) Thirty new Central universities are proposed to be established by the year 2014, 
subject to availability of resources.

6       Oral answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions 
SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, the UGC is the regulatory body which was 
established under the UGC Act 1956. It is empowered to make regulations with 
reference to ad mission and fee structure in universities and colleges also. It has been a 
body which has been issuing regulations from time to time. It issued regulations in 
1977, and in 2003 also with reference to admissions, fees and various other aspects. 
UGC also ens ures that the infrastructure is in place before it grants permission to these 
private universities.

SHRIMATI D. PURANDESWARI: Sir, from the 3 0 universities that have been 
announced by the hon. Prime Minister, 16 universities would be initially established in 
such States where no Central University actually exists. It is only after establishing 
Central Universities in these States that the other  14 would be taken into consideration. 
But, initially, the concentration would be in such States where there is no Central 
University in existence.

Sir, with regard to the withdrawal of the Private Universities Bill, this Bill was, 
actually, brought up for discussion in the Education Mnisters' meet held in January,

State Legislatures under Entry 32 of List II, Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. As 
there was no consensus on the Bill, the Bill was withdrawn.

28     Oral answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions 
SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: Sir, the hon. Minister has given a detailed 
reply to my question. ...(Interruptions)... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Please proceed with the question. 
SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH: But, Sir, the problem of shortage of power 
all over the country is a very serious problem. The Minister has given a det ailed reply 
and it is encouraging that the Eleventh Five Year Plan begins with the commissioning of 
a capacity of 1935 MW. 
Sir, my first supplementary is this. The Minister has given details about the 
completion of power projects in the country, which are not specific. I have observed that 
the completion of various projects has been very much delayed in almost all the cases 
which created a big problem in the power sector. Now, may I know from the hon. 
Minister whether the Government has formulated any speci fic programme, any specific 
scheme so that these projects, which are delayed very much, can be completed? Sir, for 
a long time, these projects have not been completed. I would like to know whether the 
Government has any specific programme to complete such projects within a stipulated 
time. 
SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE: Sir, along with my answer, I have attached 
Annexure I and II wherein the position with respect to the entire country has been given, 
not only on thermal but the details have been given with regar d to hydro also. The 
details which have been mentioned are: what is its capacity, whether it is under 
execution, what is the latest position and what are the expenses, etc. 
Everything has been mentioned in all the annexures attached to the answer. 
The second thing which he has asked is, what are the steps that the Government has 
taken to improve the position. Yes; there was a shortage. In the Ninth Plan, there was an 
energy shortage of 7.5 per cent and at the end of the Tenth Plan, the shortage was 9.6 per 
cent. The peaking shortage at the end of the Ninth Plan was 11.8 per cent and at the end 
of the Tenth Plan, it was 13.8 per cent. The capacity addition done in the Ninth Plan was 
about 19,015 MW and in the Tenth Plan, it was 21,180 MW. It is a fact, Sir, that during 
the Tenth Plan, we had targeted for about 41,110 MW, but because of the slippage and 
many other reasons, we could not achieve that target; we have achieved only 21,180 
MW. The installed capacity at the end of the Tenth Plan was 1,32,329 MW, and,  as on 
today, i.e., as per the latest figures, it is 1,35,006 MW. Sir, various steps have been 
taken. We have also received a lot of complaints and we have looked into it. If we go 
into them, the answer will be a little lengthy. But considering the positio n of the Tenth 
Plan, we have taken certain precautions. As far as the Eleventh Plan is concerned, the 
UPA Government has promised the nation that by 2012, everyone in the country will 
have, at least, one unit of electricity/household/day as a merit good. S ir, we have taken 
various steps. We have called a meeting of the State Chief Secretaries under the 
leadership of the Prime Minister, we had called the meeting of all the Chief 
Ministers/State Power Ministers and given the capacity addition for every State.  If you 
look at the capacity addition during the Seventh, Eighth and Ninth Plans, we find that it

Hiring of women and infants for begging 
*108. DR. P.C. ALEXANDER: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there has been a massive increase in the practice of hiring the services 
of women and infants by begger mafia for begging at public places in big cities of the 
country, particularly in Delhi; and 
(b) if so, the steps being taken by Government to prevent the exploitation of women 
and children by the begger mafia? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA  CHOWDHURY): (a) As informed by the 
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, the subject of beggary is a State subject 
and in the absence of relevant data/records being available in respect of beggary, it is not 
possible to indicate whether there has been an increase in the practice of hiring the 
services of women and infants by beggar mafias for begging at public places in big cities 
of the country. 
The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (Government of NCT of 
Delhi] has informed that the beggar population is a floating population and keeps 
migrating in and out of Delhi. Hence, assessment of exact number of beggars in Delhi at 
any point of time is difficult. As per a survey recently carried out by the Government of 
NCT of Delhi in all 134 M unicipal Corporation of Delhi [MCD] wards, the average 
figure was approximately 58,570 beggars in the NCT of Delhi. 
(b) According to the information given by the Ministry of Social Justice & 
Empowerment, a Central Sector Scheme had been formulated in 1992 -93, with the aim 
of providing facilities for the technical education and vocational training of beggars, 
engaging beggars in productive work so as to faciliate their reintegration into society 
and also involving voluntary welfare organizations. However, th e scheme has been 
discontinued from 1998- 99 in view of rather moderate demand from the State 
Governments/Union Territory Administrations. Presently, that Ministry is not 
implementing any scheme for curbing beggary or for welfare of beggars. 
As per the info rmation received from the Government of NCT of Delhi, regular 
enforcement action is carried out under the provisions of Bombay Prevention of 
Begging Act, 1959 as extended to Delhi to curb the practice of begging as a whole.

UNESCO's references on education in India 
*114.   SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have ascertained the references about education in the 
country in a recent publication by the International Institute of Educational Planning, an 
associate body of UNESCO; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether Government agree with such references; 

Written answers to [20 AUG., 2007] Starred questions     45 
(e) if not, whether Government have raised the issue with the concerned  
authorities in UNESCO; and 
(f) if so, the remedial steps being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ARJUN 
SINGH): (a) to (e) The Government has seen a Report published in 2007 by UNESCO/ 
International Institute of Educational Planning (HEP) entitled "Corrupt Schools, Corrupt 
Universities; what can be done?" This report is not India specific and highlights the 
issues related to corruption in education and the consequent loss to the system in terms 
of its adverse effect on access, eq uity and quality, in developed and developing 
countries around the world. The report includes references to teacher absenteeism and 
private tuitions by teachers, etc. These references have been made on the basis of a 
number of studies undertaken by differe nt researchers during the last five years or so 
and also from the Press Reports appearing from time to time. The Report also suggests 
strategies to reduce corruption and improve governance in education. Details regarding 
the references made to India in the Report are enclosed as Statement {See below). 
Though the Report has been published by UNESCO/HEP, there is a disclaimer to 
the effect that the views and opinions expressed in the report are those of the authors 
and do not necessarily represent the views of UNESCO or of the HER 
(f) Central Government is continuously engaged, through consultations with State 
Governments and apex bodies such as University Grants Commission, the Central 
Board of Secondary Education and others, in eliminating malpractices in th e 
educational system. Government of India has also commissioned an independent study 
to measure student and teacher attendance in select major States. Preliminary data frorn 
this study has shown that average teacher attendance in primary and upper primary 
schools is about 80%. Government also recognizes that eliminating the kinds of 
malpractices mentioned in the UNESCO/HEP Report will require not only the 
continuous and committed participation of State Governments but also increased public 
awareness, and greater transparency and accountability in the public bodies. 
Statement 
Details regarding the references made to India in the Report 
♦ The report presents the conclusions of the research conducted by the  
HEP in the field or ethics and corruption in education. It aims at sensitizing  
decision-makers, educational planners and managers to the importance of  
combating corruption in education; at providing them with key tools to detect 
and assess corruption problems; and at guiding them in the formulation of  
adequate strategies to curb malpractices. 
The Report is not lndia specific. However, references have been made to - 
India through out the Report. The points with reference to India are presented 
below: - 
♦ In the foreword the Report mentions that ................... Fortunately, as this 
book amply demonstrates, there are vibrant parts of sotiety — even among 

Written answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred questions 
the poorest and the most vulnerable countries like Bangladesh and India — that 
will organize in support of rational democratic and progressive dismantling of 
existing corrupt practices. 
♦ Referring to the magnitude of corruption, the Report mentions that there are a 
few estimates of the economic costs of corruption. Two national estimates of 
corruption corroborate the fact that this is major phenomenon. In India, it was 
estimated at around 20 per cent of the GNP in the 1980s. 
♦ Decision-makers in Government, academia and advocacy groups have 
come to recognize the potential of public feedback in making the 
Government more responsive and accountable. The Public Affairs 
Centre (PAC) in Bangalore, India and Transparency International 
Bangladesh (TIB), in particular, designed 'Report Cards on Public 
Services' in 2000, which prove d to be relatively uncomplicated and 
widely replicable tools for improving transparency and public 
accountability. 
♦ In the chapter titled 'Teacher management and behaviour', the 
Report opines that corrupt practices in teacher management and 
distortions in teacher behaviour can also have a high incidence on 
educational quality. 
More globally, a variety of misbehaviours associated with 
teachers can disturb the implementation of planned interventions 
within the education sector, and particularly progress toward  
Education for All goals. Any plan to increase access to education, 
improve educational quality or reduce school inequities may thus 
prove unsuccessful if it does not properly take into consideration 
issues such .as unauthorized fees for school admission, teacher -student 
relationship for private gain, and embezzlement of school finances. A 
study demonstrated, for instance, that a 10 per cent increase in teacher 
absence is associated with a 1.8 per cent decrease in student 
attendance. At the same time, anoth er study conducted by the World 
Bank showed that teacher absenteeism is not a marginal phenomenon. 
It can be as high as one third of all teachers in the State of Uttar 
Pradesh, India (World Bank, 2004). 
♦ The chapter also contains a table showing Major sources of unethical 
behaviour among teachers in South Asia. The report deals with 
'Teacher absence rate in various countries and cost implications'. India 
has also be included in the table with 25% teacher absence rate in 
primary schools with consequent budget leakage of 22,5%. 
♦ The analysis conducted by Chaudury et al (2005) in Bangladesh, India, 
Indonesia, Peru and Uganda, for instance, shows that there is no 
significant relationship between teachers' absenteeism and their 
residence with the catchments area of  school, their average tenure in 
the school and how recently they have attended a training programme.

♦ In the sub -topic 'Designing and enforcing teachers' codes of conduct', 
the Report concludes th at even though codes of conduct are generally 
perceived as useful instruments, they are not always effectively 
enforced. Various modes of enforcement have been experimented 
throughout the world, with more or less success. Existing social, 
political, cultur al and institutional factors in Bangladesh, India and 
Nepal have greatly influenced the implementation of these codes. 
♦ In the chapter-7 which deals with exams, credentials and accreditation, 
the Report mentions that in some places in India, cheating is now  so 
well established that when Universities try to resist, students protest 
and demand their traditional right to cheat. In the Report, some 
examples of academic fraud have been mentioned. One of them is 
related to the findings of The Commission of Investi gation on Abuse 
of Authority in Nepal, which suspects that 10% of the Himalayan 
Kingdom's 1,40,000 school teachers are using diplomas purchased 
from India (Chronicle of Higher Education, 2003). Similarly, some 
press reports on figures on academic fraud hav e been included, which 
are as under:- 
lndia: fees for manipulating entrance tests scores between USS 80 and 
USS 20,000 for the most popular programmes, such as computer 
sciences, medicine or engineering. 
India: Post dated cheques totalling more than US$300,000 collected 
by people offering to sell answers for a nationwide examinations for 
physicians. 
♦ In the chapter titled 'Private tutoring: How to avoid the corruption of 
mainstream education?', the Report mentions that according to a recent 
comparative study  undertaken, by the IIEP on teachers codes of 
conduct in South Asia, private tuition is thus regarded as a major 
source of unethical behaviour in Bangladesh, India and Nepal. 
♦ The Report also says that in India, a 1997 survey of 7,879 primary 
schools pupils  in Delhi found that 39.2 per cent were receiving 
tutoring. Other reports have suggested that 70 per cent of urban 
children receive private tutoring in one or more subjects. 
♦ In the chapter regarding memo to policy makers, planners and 
managers on how to ad dress the challenge of corruption in the 
Education Sector, there is a subtopic titled 'How to address external 
factors (mainly political, legal, economical and educational)'. 
This chapter mentions that lessons from experience and 
evidence suggest that five  key elements hold a lot of promise when 
they can coalesce, namely, leadership; competition in the political and 
economic arena; the right to information; collective action; and an 
integrated approach.

Research studies on global warming 
744. SHRI. C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of EARTH SCIENCES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the research institutes under the Ministry are working in a coordinated 
manner to resolve issues pertaining to global warming, that are either dir ectly or 
indirectly affecting the socio-economic growth of the country; 
(b) if so, whether research studies are done on melting down of Himalayan Glaciers, 
increased occurrence of cyclone, particularly in Andhra Pradesh, flash floods, cloud 
bursts, etc; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; along with the breakthrough made, if any; and 
(d) if not, the reasons thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF EARTH SCIENCES (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes, Sir.  
The India Meteorological Department (IMD), the Indian Institute of Tropical 
Meteorology (IITM) , and other concerned institutes of the Ministry are working in a 
coordinated manner to address the science issues related to global warming. Wadia 
Institute of Himalayan Geology(WIHG) is also pursuing research related to climate 
change/global warming usin g the various proxies and geological records. The findings 
on trends of climate change over the Indian region have formed the basis for further 
impact studies on socio-economic aspects carried out by other research groups. 
(b) and (c) Several studies have been undertaken by the IITM, Pune, National Centre 
for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF) and IMD on the cyclonic 
disturbances that form in Bay of Bengal and cross Andhra Coast. In general it was 
observed that the number of intense storms (monsoon depressions) that form over the 
Bay of Bengal have been showing a decline during the past 2 -3 decades while there is a 
general increasing trend in the low -pressure systems (low -intensity). There are no 
conclusive results yet obtained on trends of flash floods and cloud bursts.  
It is well-established fact that glaciers, in general, including the Himalayan glaciers, 
recede or build -up in response to variations in temperature of the region in which they 
are located. The analysis of temperature data for more tha n a century indicates slight 
increase of temperature, particularly in the winter season over the Western Himalayan 
region with some local variations. The recession in glaciers could be attributed to 
various reasons, including the possibility due to global warming. In the past 7,50,000 
years, there have been Ice Age cycles, separated by warmer periods 

Written answers to [20 AUG, 2007] Unstarred questions     57 
called interglacial periods. This is part of the normal climate variation cycle. The effects 
of Greenhouse warming, if any. shall be superimposed on such natural variations. Due 
to such complexities it is difficult to make clear attribution of the observed recession of 
Himalayan glaciers to global warming. 
(d) Does not arise.

Electrification of villages in Bihar 
827. SHRI MOTTIUR RAHMAN: Will the Minister of NEW AND RENEWABLE 
ENERGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a vast majority of rural population still has no access to electricity and is 
dependent on kerosene lamps and lanterns; 
(b) if so, the schemes formula ted for electrification of 25,000 remote villages/ 
hamlets; 
(c) the reasons for not electrifying even a single remote village of Bihar under the 
Remote Village Electrification Programme by the 30th November, 2004; and  
(d) the list of 273 remote villages of the Sta te identified for electrification under the 
programme, district-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NEW AND RENEWABLE 
ENERGY (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) As per the Office Memorandum dated 
18th March, 2005, issued by Ministry of Power for Rajeev Gandhi Grameen 
Vidyutikaran Yojana, out of 13.8 crore rural house holds in the country, around 7.8 
crore rural house holds (as per 2001 census) do not have access to electricity and may 
thus have to depend upon alternatives such as kerosene lamps and lante rns for 
illumination. 
(b to (d) A Programme for financial support of upto 90% of the costs of projects for 
electrification through renewable sources of energy of remote unelectrified census 
villages and unelectrified hamlets of electrified census villages,  is being implemented by 
the Ministry. The number of such villages was tentatively arrived at 24418 before 2005 -
06 on the basis of information provided by the states. This included a list of 273 villages 
in 23 districts of Bihar submitted by the State Gove rnment. After initiation of the Rajiv 
Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana by the Ministry of Power, only those 
villages/hamlets where grid connectivity is either not feasible or not cost effective will 
be covered under the Remote Village Electrification Pro gramme. The task of 
identification of such villages has been entrusted to the Rural Electrification Corporation 
who have so far identified 72 such villages in West Champaran District of Bihar. The 
State Government has been advised to submit proposals for c overage of these villages 
under the Programme. However, no such proposal has so far been received.

the rural remote areas and hilly terrain in the countr y, in a cost effective and 
environmentally benign manner; and

Study on hydro power dams 
834. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are studying the points raised by some 
countries on the hydro power dams; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the present status of each dam? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL KUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) Under 
the provisions of the Indus Waters Treaty 1960 between India and Pakistan, India is 
required to furnish information in respect of new run- of-river projects (including Small 
Plants) and Storage Projects on Western Rivers i.e. (Jhelum, Chenab & Indus and their 
tributaries). As informed by the Ministry of Water Resources, information in respect of 
28 projects has so far been sent to Pakistan which had raised objections on each of them 
but has been pursuing them vigorously only in respect of a few projects namely 
Kishanganga, Uri -II (both under construction) and the Baglihar Hydro Electric (HE) 
Project mentioned below. India has been examining the ob jections and endeavoring to 
resolve them through correspondence and meetings of the Permanent Indus Commission 
within the purview of the Treaty and Secretary Level Talks, as decided between the two 
Governments. 
The Ministry of Water Resources have also inf ormed that Pakistan had points of 
difference related to India's design of Baglihar HE Project over the river Chenab in 
Jammu & Kashmir (J&K) with regard to freeboard, provision of pondage, provision of 
gates & low level spillways and the level of intakes. Government of Pakistan had 
referred these points of differences to the World Bank in January 2005 for examination 
by a Neutral Expert. The Neutral Expert appointed by the World Bank has since given 
his Expert Determination on 12.2.2007 which is final and binding on both the countries. 
The project is currently under construction.

Status of UMPP at Sasan 
836. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that for the last six months, the country's largest Greenfield 
power project is on standby mode; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that six mo nths after it chose a bidder for the 4000 MW 
Ultra Mega Power project (UMPP) at Sasan in Madhya Pradesh and gave it a Letter of 
Intent, the Ministry now cannot decide whether or not to award the contract; and  
(c) if so, whether Government have made any investi gations in this matter and if so, 
the action proposed thereon? 

128   Written answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred questions 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHIL .KUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) The 
transfer of the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPYV) that is, Sasan Power  Limited (SPL) to 
the bidder identified for implementation of the 4000 MW Sasan Ultra Mega Power 
Project in Madhya Pradesh had been held up after issue of the Letter of Intent on 
account of legal and contractual issues. The Empowered Group of Ministers (EG oM), 
set up for facilitating expeditious decisions in all cases concerning Ultra Mega Power 
Projects (UMPPs), examined the matter relating to the award of the project. 
Keeping in view the overall public interest and after examination of various clauses 
of the bid documents, the EGoM inter -alia decided that the procurer should cancel the 
Letter of Intent issued to the Globeleq -Lanco consortium, as the consortium was not 
qualified even at the RfQ stage and its response to the RfQ was void ab- initio. It also 
decided that the procurer should return the Bid Bond of the consortium after deducting a 
sum of Rs.l crore, and hold negotiations with the remaining bidders and seek their final 
bid(s) for levelised tariff. 
Accordingly, Sasan Power Limited (SPL) received revised offers from the remaining 
valid bidders, of which the bid of M/s. Reliance Power Limited, offering a levellised 
tariff of Rs. 1.19616 per kilo watt hour was the lowest. SPL issued the Letter of Intent to 
M/s. Reliance Power Limited on 1st August, 200 7, and has thereafter carried out the 
necessary documentation on 7th August, 2007 for the transfer to them of the Special 
Purpose Vehicle, Sasan Power Limited which had been set up for the Sasan UMPP.

845. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased  to 
state: 
(a) whether the Tala Transmission System a joint venture between the Power Grid 
Corporation of India Limited and Power Links Transmission Limited, the first Public -
Private Partnership in Power Sector, was recently inaugurated by Prime Minister in 
North East; 
(b) if so, the details of enhanced National Grid capacity with improved security, 
stability and reliability; 
(c) the likely cost of this first capacity link; and 
(d) the time -frame with in which this economic exchange of power would lead to 
recovery of the entire cost of the project? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) The Prime 
Minister of India dedicated the "East -North Tala Transmission System" to the Nation on 
20.06.2007. 
(b) With the commissioning of the above transmission system, the ca pacity of the 
National Grid (inter-regional power transfer capacity) has been enhanced by 2000 MW. 
The present aggregate capacity is 14600 MW.

(c) The cost of the project is approximately Rs.2800 crore. 
(d) As decided by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC), the

the project is about 35 years.

Power subsidy 
848. SHRI AMAR SINGH: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have calculated the power subsidy to be given to PSUs, in 
the event of a multifold rise in the sale price of gas; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) in what manner Government have decided to absorb the excess expenditure, 
consequent on the rise in the sale price of gas? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) to (c) At 
present, two part tariff structure is applicable to Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs). 
This consists of firstly the fixed cost, which mainly covers debt servicing and 
repayment, return on equity etc. and of the variable cost, which mainly covers the fuel 
cost. Any increase or decrease in the variable cost on account of change in the fuel cost

Unscheduled power cuts in Delhi  
851. SHRI AMIR ALAM KHAN: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that unscheduled power cut is characteristic in the capital, 
which perhaps is in violation of the Indian Electricity Act; 
(b) whether Government are aware that despite being the capital city, Delhi is short 
of power and even then it is selling power to other States; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that power distribution companies are supplying power 
to villages of States bordering Delhi, because they get an opportunity to charge higher 
tariff from them; and 
(d) if so, the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SUSHILKUMAR SHINDE): (a) Under Section 
42 of the Electricity Act 2003, it is "the duty of a Distribution Licensee to develop and 
maintain an efficient, co -ordinated and economical distribution system in his area of 
supply." However, u nscheduled power cuts are resorted to at times due to a variety of 
reasons like sudden drop in generation, drop in the grid frequency, outages in the 
transmission and distribution network, etc. 
(b) According to the Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission, ther e have been 
instances where Delhi has sold power to other States but this has been done during those 
time slots when Delhi was surplus in power. 
(c) and (d) It is informed by The Government of NCT of Delhi that the Discoms are 
supplying power in the licensed a rea of power supply and no power is supplied to 
villages of States bordering Delhi.

861 SHRI A. VIJYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether CSIR/IGIB is associated with The Centre for Genomic Applications 
(TCGA); 
(b) if so, the details thereof, including other organizations associated with TCGA, 
amount of financial support provided to TCGA, income generated by TCGA, procedure 
adopted to appoint various employees working at TCGA, designation and basic 
pay/consolidated p ay fixed against various positions on which employees/ consultants 
are working/associated at TCGA during the last three years, year -wise, organization -
wise, category-wise, position-wise; and 
(c) the text of the agreement signed by CSIR/IGIB with other agencies  by which 
TCGA had been established? 
THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes 
Sir. 
(b) TCGA is a collaborative project between CSIR/IGIB (Institute of Genomics & 
Integrative Biology, Delhi, a National laboratory under CSIR) and In stitute of Molecular 
Medicine (1MM), Kolkata, a section 25 not -for-Profit company to create and operate 
core shared facility for Genomics and Proteomics to assist in drug discovery. TCGA also 
provides life sciences services in this area. 
The mandate of TCGA is: 
• To create necessary infrastructure and work ambience, on par with the 
international research facilities. 
• To catalyze genomic revolution in Indian R&D sector to bring affordable 
healthcare benefit to the people of lndia with a focus on the discovery o f 
new molecular and predictive medicine in the post genomic sequencing era. 
• To operate as a national co -share resource and facility for use by 
Universities, Industry, small laboratories and research groups in National 
Laboratories thereby enabling the coun try to do more with less budgetary 
support. 

Written answers to [20 AUG., 2007] Unstarred questions   175 
• To make research in the frontier areas of biological sciences affordable and 
accessible to larger section of stakeholders and empower them to take 
advantage of facilities at the cutting edge of technologies to make new 
discoveries. 
• To provide state -of-the art environment and infrastructure as 
"Incubators/Start-up' to scientist entrepreneurs. 
• To spur business, entrepreneurial, and employment opportunities. 
Aims and objectives 
TCGA has been established with state -of-the art facilities, to cut down the research 
time and costs that is necessary to position India as Global player in life science research. 
TCGA aims to liberate scientists from mundane activities of managing research facilities 
and to provide cost effective and quality services through centralized operations, due to 
economy of scale and operational excellence. 
Financial support provided to TCGA 
No direct financial support is provided to TCGA/IMM. However, equipment procured by 
IGIB through funding from DST of Rs. 8.25 crores and CSIR of Rs. 2.72 crores for National

considered that given the longitudinal difference between the extreme regions in the 
country, technically it is possible to have two time zones. But these will be 5 hours and 
6 hours ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) respectively, in place of the present

international norms. However, it was noted that this will enable savings in daylight 
hours only by half an hour for the eastern States, whereas there will be a corresponding 
loss of half an hour in the Central and the Western States. The Committee observed that 
this does not provide any major advantage, yet on the other hand, pose several 
difficulties in terms of differential timings for airlines, Railways, radio and TV, STD 
services etc. A more prudent and effective solution

Selection of NGOs for grant-in-aid 
872. KUMARI NIRMALA DESHPANDE: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE  
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the reasons for surrendering the right to select NGOs for grant -in-aid scheme to 
the State Governments; and 
(b) whether NGOs have willingly accepted this decision? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND 
EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI SUBBULAKSHMI JAGADEESAN) (a) and (b) In the 
past, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment received the applications of the 
NGOs from the State Governments with their recommendations. This procedure has not 
changed. 
Procedure for examining the proposals of NGOs in the Ministry too has not changed. 
However, the procedure for sanction of grant -in-aid to NGOs has been streamlined from 
current financial year. This was necessitated because recommendation of the State 
Governments for NGOs were being received in a piecemeal manner. In several cases, 
they got delayed resulting in late release of funds to NGOs. The old procedure had also 
created varying asymmetry in the fund flow to various States. 
The streamlining would result in submission of recommendations for NGOs by the 
State Governments in a consolidated manner by a definite time limit.

SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:

Women trafficking across Nepal and Bangladesh 
877. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD  
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that around 20,000 to 25,000 women are trafficked  every year 
across Nepal and Bangladesh borders; 
(b) if so, how long this problem would subsist and whether it is on the increase or 
decrease; 
(c) the measures taken to curb and control this problem; and 
(d) whether the measures taken are adequate and effective? 
THE M INISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) There is no 
accurate data available on cross border trafficking. However, as per the Action Research 
on Trafficking in Women and Children Study of National Human Rights Commission in 
collaboration with UNIFEM and the Institute of Social Sciences released in 2004, it is 
estimated that about 5,000 to 10,000 girls are being annually trafficked from Nepal and 
Bangladesh into India. 
(c) and (d) As per informa tion received from Ministry of Home Affairs "Police" and 
"Public Order" are State subjects, and the State Governments are primarily responsible 
for prevention and combating of crime of human trafficking. However, the Union 
Government is taking several meas ures, in concert with the State Government's for 
prevention and control of crime of trafficking as well as measures for rehabilitation of 
victims. The Union Government has advised all the State Governments to deal with the 
crime of trafficking in a holistic manner.

Problems of women being trafficked 
884. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD  
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the position of the problems of women being trafficked within the country; 
(b) whether this problem has been taken serious cognizance by Government; and 
(c) the rescue and rehabilitation measures for victims? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) to (c) A study  
commissioned by Ministry of Women and Child Development on 'Girls and Women  
in Prostitution in India' and conducted by Gram Niyojan Kendra, 2004, shows that  
significant number of women are trafficked withi n the country for Commercial Sexual  
Exploitation. Ministry of Women and Child Development runs Swadhar Shelter  
Homes which provide shelter, food, clothing, emotional support, counselling,  
rehabilitation and other facilities to women in difficult circumstan ces including  
victims of trafficking. A Pilot Project on combating trafficking of women and children  
for sexual exploitation is also being implemented. A 'Comprehensive Scheme for  
Prevention of Trafficking and Rescue, Rehabilitation and re -integration of V ictims of  
Trafficking and Commercial Sexual Exploitation' has been included in the Annual Plan  
2007-08. The scheme has specific components for prevention of trafficking, rescue,  
rehabilitation and repatriation of victims. The Central Advisory Committee on  
combating Child Prostitution headed by Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child  
Development, Government of India reviews the State's activities in combating  
trafficking and prostitution every quarter. The Ministry of Women and Child  
Development also conducts  advocacy, awareness generation, sensitisation  
programme for prevention of trafficking.

WHO standards on child growth 
897. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
Will the Minister of WOMEN AND CHILD DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have adopted the new WHO standards on child growth, 
that may help improve our poor rating on the global child nourishment index; 
(b) if so, whether cases of malnutrition of children in Vidarbha region and the 
judgement of Bombay High Court in this matter have been taken into account; 
(c) whether Government have seen the survey conducted by the Right to Food 
campaign, which was conducted in six States; and 
(d) if so, what are their views on the observation made therein? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WOMEN AND CHILD 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) and (b) The Ministry of 
Women and Child Developme nt has taken a decision to adopt the new WHO Child 
Growth Standards in Integrated Child Development Services which may marginally 
improve our poor rating on global child nutrition scenario. The new WHO -Child Growth 
Standards are based on a multi -centric study carried out in six countries including India. 
These are scientific, gender specific and for the first time describe, 

210   Written answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred questions 
"how children should grow". The standard formulation utilizes growth of hea lthy 
children only. Hence the question of taking into account the cases of malnutrition of 
children in Vidarbha region or the judgement of Bombay High Court in this matter does 
not arise. 
(c) Yes, Sir. The Survey Report titled "Focus on children under Six", br ought out by 
the Citizens Initiatives for the Rights of Children under Six, indicated a decline in the 
qualitative aspects of the programme in some of the States/UTs. 
(d) Taking a serious view of the observations made therein, the Hon'ble Prime 
Minister in a letter to the Chief Ministers, impressed upon them the need to set up an 
institutional review process at their level after carrying out a detailed assessment of the 
Programme in their State; lay emphasis on the programme status in areas with 
concentaration of minority communities and preponderance of Scheduled Castes and 
Tribes, adequately empower Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) and Urban Local Bodies 
(ULBs) to monitor and supervise the working of these Committees; make line officials 
firmly accountable f or their action and report on a quarterly basis on further 
developments in this sector.

RULING BY THE CHAIR 
Conversion of privilege notices into discussion under rule 176 on Indo-
US Civil Nuclear Co-operation Agreement 
MR. CHAIRMAN: The Chair has to give a ruling on notices given under Rule 168. I 
have receiv ed several notices under Rule 168 on matters pertaining to the Indo- US 
Nuclear Agreement. On scrutiny of these notices, I have found that in some of the 
motions, a demand has been made for disapproval or rejection of the Agreement or have 
a vote of the Hou se on it. In other cases, a demand has been made for renegotiation of 
the Agreement. There are other notices of motion, again under Rule 168, in which a 
demand has been made to have a discussion on the Agreement. Since it is not a 
Constitutional obligatio n for the Executive to have the approval of Parliament on any 
international treaty or agreement, admission of these motions which involve approval of 
Parliament would not be in order. I am, therefore, converting these notices into notices 
for discussion under Rule 176. The Business Advisory Committee has already identified 
this subject for discussion.
